I know it sounds odd, but it would quietly make my day if the Moon happened to be impossible to see right now.

I'm in Reykjavik, Iceland at 2026-03-23 20:13 GMT (UTC+0000) (2026-03-23T20:13:00Z in UTC), at latitude 64.1466 degrees and longitude -21.9426 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is -2.433 degrees and its azimuth is 279.292 degrees, so it is below the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 44.527 degrees and its azimuth is 231.781 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 28.23 percent illuminated, 64.075 degrees from the Sun, and 363205.2 kilometers away. The sky brightness is civil twilight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes — very likely.

At 44.5° altitude, the Moon is well above the horizon, and a 28%-illuminated crescent/gibbous Moon is normally easy to see with the naked eye in clear conditions. Its angular separation from the Sun is about 64°, so it is not buried in the immediate bright twilight glow near the Sun.

Civil twilight does make the sky bright, especially with the Sun only about 2.4° below the horizon, but the Moon should still be visible to a normal observer who knows where to look. It will be toward azimuth ~232° — southwest — and fairly high in the sky, roughly halfway between the horizon and zenith.

The main caveat is that it may not jump out instantly against the bright blue twilight sky. Scan slowly around that southwest, 45°-high area; once located, it should be plainly visible.
